title: Title, date and the opening
short: Title from Edgar's mad song in King Lear 3.4; written in one day, 2 January 1852, in Paris, and published in Men and Women (1855).
body: In King Lear Edgar, disguised as the madman Poor Tom, sings a scrap of ballad: 'Child Rowland to the dark tower came'. Browning took this line, which has no known story behind it, and invented the quest leading to it. He wrote the poem on 2 January 1852 in Paris, having resolved to write a poem every day; according to DeVane and later accounts, he said it came upon him 'as a kind of dream'. It was published in Men and Women (1855). In his later collected editions Browning regrouped his shorter poems, and this one came to sit among the 'Dramatic Romances', which may explain the archive's label; it was not in the 1845 Dramatic Romances and Lyrics. The opening 'My first thought' implies thoughts after it: the knight is recalling the journey.

sources.cite: Shakespeare, King Lear 3.4 (Edgar as Poor Tom: 'Child Rowland to the dark tower came')

title: the hoary cripple
short: The grey, malicious guide whose directions Roland follows though he believes them lies; the poem's first figure of the hostile world.
body: 'Hoary' means grey or white with age. The cripple is a familiar romance figure, the wayside guide, made sinister. Roland reads malice into his eye and his half-suppressed glee, yet does what he says. The paradox sets up the poem's psychology: the quester expects deceit and failure and goes on anyway. Since everything is filtered through Roland's suspicion, some critics ask whether the cripple really lies at all, since the path does lead to the Tower. The 'staff' and 'crutch' that 'gin write my epitaph' (st. 2) turn the guide into a figure of death.

title: Stanza and metre
short: Thirty-four six-line stanzas of iambic pentameter rhyming abbaab: the returning a-rhyme gives each stanza a closed, trapped circularity.
body: Each stanza rhymes abbaab (word / eye / lie / afford / scored / thereby). The first rhyme sound returns twice, enclosing the middle, so each stanza circles back on itself as the knight's journey does. Browning often runs sentences across stanza breaks (sts. 2-3, 5-6, 20-21), so the form pulls one way and the syntax another, a restless forward movement inside closed units. The rhymes are often harsh or grotesque (stanza 25's 'mirth' / 'earth' / 'dearth'), matching the landscape. Thirty-four stanzas make 204 lines.

sources.cite: Norton Anthology of English Literature, vol. E (The Victorian Age), notes to 'Childe Roland'
William Clyde DeVane, A Browning Handbook, 2nd ed. (Appleton-Century-Crofts, 1955), entry on 'Childe Roland'

title: the dying man's overheard funeral
short: An extended simile: like a dying man who overhears plans for his burial and fears only to 'shame' the mourners by living, Roland half-wishes to fail.
body: The two-stanza simile is bitterly comic. The dying man hears his friends discuss graves, banners and the best day for 'carrying the corpse away', and his only wish is not to embarrass them by surviving. Roland's quest has become something like that: he has heard failure foretold so often that failure seems the fitting end. The simile turns the heroic quest into an image of shame and social expectation. Bloom reads such moments as signs of Roland's self-destructive wish; others see a stoic acceptance of death.

sources.cite: Harold Bloom, 'Browning's Childe Roland: All Things Deformed and Broken', in The Ringers in the Tower (U of Chicago P, 1971)
William Clyde DeVane, A Browning Handbook, 2nd ed. (Appleton-Century-Crofts, 1955), entry on 'Childe Roland'

title: 'The Band'
short: The fellowship of knights who have sought the Dark Tower and failed; Roland's question is not whether he will succeed but whether he is 'fit' to fail like them.
body: The quotation marks make 'The Band' sound like a formal title, a roll-call of failed questers. Roland's ambition has turned around: 'just to fail as they, seemed best'. The idea of a company of knights questing for a secret place recalls Arthurian Grail romance. In the last stanzas these lost knights, 'my peers', reappear ranged along the hills to watch his end (st. 34). Several critics, notably Bloom, read the Band as poetic precursors, earlier poets whose failures the latecomer both honours and fears.

sources.cite: Harold Bloom, 'Browning's Childe Roland: All Things Deformed and Broken', in The Ringers in the Tower (U of Chicago P, 1971)

title: estray
short: A legal term for a stray domestic animal found wandering without an owner; the dim day 'leers' to see the plain claim its stray.
body: 'Estray' comes from law: a valuable tame animal found wandering, which could be claimed by the lord of the manor. Browning makes Roland himself the 'estray' and the plain its new owner. The sunset is personified as giving 'one grim / Red leer' of satisfaction. The legal word makes the capture sound official and impersonal. The next stanza makes the trap literal: as soon as Roland is 'pledged to the plain', the road behind him vanishes.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'estray, n.'
Norton Anthology of English Literature, vol. E (The Victorian Age), notes to 'Childe Roland'

title: cockle, spurge
short: Weeds of cornfields: cockle (corn-cockle, a poisonous weed) and spurge (plants with acrid milky sap); even these merely 'propagate their kind'.
body: Corn-cockle grows among wheat and its seeds are poisonous. In the KJV Job swears, 'let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley' (Job 31:40). Spurge (Euphorbia) has an irritant, milky juice. The land is 'starved' and 'ignoble'; flowers are as unlikely as a cedar grove, and a burr would be 'treasure trove'. Browning's grotesque nature is a deliberate anti-pastoral. Bloom, following DeVane, connects it with Gerard de Lairesse's Art of Painting, which Browning read as a boy and which has a chapter on 'things deformed and broken'.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Job 31:40

title: 'It nothing skills' and the Last Judgment's fire
short: 'It nothing skills' = it makes no difference; Nature herself says only the fire of Judgment Day can cure the land, burning its clods to ash.
body: 'Skill' as an impersonal verb ('it skills not') meant 'it matters' or 'it makes a difference'; The older impersonal use survives in Browning's day mainly in verse. Here a petulant Nature admits she cannot help her case. Only the 'Last Judgment's fire' can 'calcine its clods', that is, burn them to powder or quicklime, as in chemistry, and 'set my prisoners free'. The image draws on 2 Peter 3:10, where 'the elements shall melt with fervent heat'. A suffering creation waiting for release also recalls Romans 8:22.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'skill, v.1'
The Bible (KJV), 2 Peter 3:10
The Bible (KJV), Romans 8:22

title: bents ... Pashing
short: 'Bents' are stiff coarse grasses; 'pashing' (dialect) means smashing or crushing, as if some brute had trampled the dock leaves.
body: Bent grass is the wiry grass of heaths and dunes. Browning imagines the thistle's head 'chopped' because the bents 'were jealous', so even the weeds act out envy. The dock's 'swarth' (dark) leaves are torn and 'bruised'. 'Pash' is an old word, probably imitative, meaning to strike violently or smash; Shakespeare's Ajax threatens to 'pash' Achilles o'er the face (Troilus and Cressida 2.3). Roland infers 'a brute' with 'a brute's intents', inventing malice where he sees only damage. This habit is typical of the poem.

title: the stiff blind horse
short: The poem's most famous grotesque: a gaunt, half-dead horse, 'Thrust out past service from the devil's stud!', which Roland hates as if its pain proved guilt.
body: The horse is said to derive from a figure in a tapestry that hung in Browning's Florence home (now at Balliol College, Oxford). 'Colloped' neck means thick with folds of flesh: 'collops' are slices of meat, and Job 15:27 speaks of the wicked man who 'maketh collops of fat on his flanks'. 'Stud' is a stable of horses kept for breeding. The striking moral turn comes at the close of st. 14: 'He must be wicked to deserve such pain.' Roland reverses cause and effect, a reflex that critics read as a sign of his warped perception or of a cruel universe that makes suffering look like guilt.

title: Cuthbert
short: A fellow knight remembered for comfort, until memory of 'one night's disgrace' spoils it; the name is a saint's, ironically.
body: Roland, like a soldier calling for wine before battle, tries to draw courage from 'earlier, happier sights'. The first, golden-haired Cuthbert linking arms with him, collapses at once with 'one night's disgrace', never explained. The name belongs to St Cuthbert of Lindisfarne, the Northumbrian saint, which sharpens the irony of the shame. Browning leaves the disgrace untold. The unexplained hints are part of what makes the poem dreamlike and open to interpretation.

sources.cite: William Clyde DeVane, A Browning Handbook, 2nd ed. (Appleton-Century-Crofts, 1955), entry on 'Childe Roland'
Norton Anthology of English Literature, vol. E (The Victorian Age), notes to 'Childe Roland'

anchor: Giles then, the soul of honor
title: Giles and the traitor's parchment
short: A second friend, once 'the soul of honor', is remembered branded a traitor, a placard pinned to his breast by the hangman.
body: Giles' motto is reported in a deliberately tangled line: 'What honest man should dare (he said) he durst.' He would dare anything an honest man should dare. Then the 'scene shifts' to his public disgrace: hangman's hands pin a 'parchment' (a written charge) to his breast. Condemned men were sometimes paraded with their crime written on a placard. 'His own bands' (his own company) read it. Both memories show honour turning to shame. Roland concludes, 'Better this present than a past like that.'

sources.cite: William Clyde DeVane, A Browning Handbook, 2nd ed. (Appleton-Century-Crofts, 1955), entry on 'Childe Roland'
Norton Anthology of English Literature, vol. E (The Victorian Age), notes to 'Childe Roland'

title: the sudden little river
short: A spiteful black stream, like a bath for the 'fiend's glowing hoof'; fording it, Roland fears corpses underfoot and spears something that shrieks like a baby.
body: The river appears 'as unexpected as a serpent comes', a hint of Eden's tempter. It is 'petty yet so spiteful', with alders kneeling and willows flinging themselves in 'mute despair, a suicidal throng'. The landscape is again moralised as cruelty and suffering. 'Bespate' means spattered. Crossing a river is a traditional threshold in quest and underworld journeys (compare Styx and Acheron). The water-rat with 'a baby's shriek' is the poem's most shocking moment of uncertainty: Roland cannot tell what he has killed.

sources.cite: Norton Anthology of English Literature, vol. E (The Victorian Age), notes to 'Childe Roland'

title: fell cirque ... horrid mews
short: Cirque: a circular arena; mews: an enclosure (originally a cage for moulting hawks). Roland imagines a battle fought in a trampled ring with no exit.
body: 'Fell' means fierce or deadly. 'Cirque' (from Latin circus) is an arena, and 'mews' were the cages where hawks were kept while moulting (Old French mue, from muer, 'to moult'). Roland pictures 'toads in a poisoned tank' or 'wild cats in a red-hot iron cage'. The simile then turns to Turkish galleys, where slaves were supposedly set to fight 'Christians against Jews' for the master's sport. The scene has no footprints in or out, so the violence is sealed off from any cause, which matches the dream logic of the poem.

title: Tophet's tool
short: Tophet, the place in the valley of Hinnom where children were burned to Molech; it came to mean hell. The wheel or harrow looks like hell's torture engine.
body: In the Old Testament, Tophet in the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem was where children were 'burned in the fire' as sacrifices (Jeremiah 7:31; 2 Kings 23:10). It became a byword for hell, as in Milton's Paradise Lost 1.404-5. Roland sees an 'engine', a wheel, a 'brake' (an instrument of torture), a 'harrow fit to reel / Men's bodies out like silk'. He thinks it might be a hellish tool left on earth, or brought up 'to sharpen its rusty teeth of steel'. The image recalls the medieval 'harrowing of hell' and instruments of martyrdom.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Jeremiah 7:31

title: rood
short: A small measure (a rod, about 5.5 yards, or a quarter-acre); in so short a space the ground runs through bog, clay, rubble and sand.
body: 'Rood' as a measure meant a rod or perch of land, and also a quarter of an acre; the same word means the Cross ('Holy Rood'). The point is the speed of the degradation: within a few yards the land runs through every kind of waste, ending in 'stark black dearth'. The parenthesis before it compares nature to a fool who makes a thing and then mars it until his mood changes, an image of a capricious creator. Critics have related this to Browning's later grotesque theologies, such as 'Caliban upon Setebos'.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'rood, n.'

title: Apollyon's bosom-friend
short: Apollyon is the angel of the abyss in Revelation 9:11 and Christian's dragon-winged foe in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress; the black bird is his companion.
body: Revelation 9:11 names the king of the bottomless pit 'in the Hebrew tongue Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue... Apollyon', meaning Destroyer. In Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress (1678) Christian fights Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation: a monster with scales like a fish and 'wings like a dragon'. Hence the bird's 'wide wing dragon-penned' (with dragon's feathers or pinions). Roland's quest has often been compared to Christian's pilgrimage, though here the landscape gives no promise of the Celestial City. The bird's brushing pass may be 'the guide I sought'.

title: 'came a click / As when a trap shuts'
short: The plain has become a ring of mountains without his noticing; the sound of a trap shutting marks recognition: 'This was the place!'
body: The mountains have 'stolen in view', and Roland half-recognises the trick from 'a bad dream perhaps'. The 'click' is a striking modern, mechanical image in a romance landscape. The trap shutting turns the long search into sudden arrival, and arrival into capture. 'In the very nick / Of giving up' means at the exact critical moment. Compare 'Estray' (st. 8), where the plain caught its stray, and the road behind that vanished.

sources.cite: Norton Anthology of English Literature, vol. E (The Victorian Age), notes to 'Childe Roland'

title: Dunce, / Dotard
short: Roland curses himself as a fool for nearly missing the place he trained all his life to see; 'dunce' derives from the philosopher Duns Scotus.
body: Humanists and reformers mocked the followers of the scholastic theologian John Duns Scotus as 'Dunsmen' or 'dunses', and the word came to mean a dull-witted person. 'Dotard' is one in his dotage; 'at the very nonce' means at the very moment. The self-reproach breaks off mid-line as the hills are described ('a tall scalped mountain ... Dunce'), so the syntax registers the shock of recognition. 'Burningly' opening the stanza makes the realisation feel like fire.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'dunce, n.'
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'nonce, n.'

title: the Tower itself
short: The goal turns out to be squat, brown and 'blind as the fool's heart', like a hidden reef the sailor sees only when his ship strikes it.
body: After the epic build-up the Tower is anticlimactic: round, squat, brown stone, 'without a counterpart / In the whole world'. 'Blind as the fool's heart' recalls Psalm 14:1, 'The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God'. The simile of the 'tempest's mocking elf' who points the sailor to the 'unseen shelf' (a sandbank or reef) only as 'the timbers start' (spring apart) makes recognition and ruin happen at once. Critics have related the Tower to death, to the poet's self, or to the unknowable object of any quest; Browning refused to explain.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Psalm 14:1
Harold Bloom, 'Browning's Childe Roland: All Things Deformed and Broken', in The Ringers in the Tower (U of Chicago P, 1971)
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'shelf, n.2'

title: the hills like giants at a hunting
short: The hills lie 'Chin upon hand' like giant hunters watching a stag at bay and calling for the kill: 'to the heft!' (up to the hilt).
body: Roland now becomes the hunted 'creature', the animal brought to bay. The giants' cry 'Now stab and end the creature—to the heft!' (the heft is the handle or hilt of a knife) puts the hunting ritual of the kill into a cosmic frame. The dying sunset returns to light the scene, so nothing is hidden: 'Not see? ... Not hear?' The questions answer an imagined objection, as if the reader suggested that Roland might have missed the Tower in the dark. The landscape's watching faces prepare for the assembled Band.

sources.cite: Norton Anthology of English Literature, vol. E (The Victorian Age), notes to 'Childe Roland'

anchor: all the lost adventurers my peers
title: the lost adventurers, 'a living frame'
short: The names of the dead knights toll like a bell, and they stand along the hills 'to view the last of me', framing him like a picture.
body: Sound swells 'like a bell', a death knell made of names. The lost knights were strong, bold or fortunate, 'yet each of old / Lost, lost!' Then they appear 'ranged along the hillsides', a 'living frame / For one more picture'. The language of painting (frame, picture, sheet of flame) makes Roland's last act a scene to be watched. Bloom reads the peers as precursor poets; others as the communion of failed heroes whom Roland joins in a final act of courage. The flame recalls the Last Judgment's fire of stanza 11.

sources.cite: Harold Bloom, 'Browning's Childe Roland: All Things Deformed and Broken', in The Ringers in the Tower (U of Chicago P, 1971)
William Clyde DeVane, A Browning Handbook, 2nd ed. (Appleton-Century-Crofts, 1955), entry on 'Childe Roland'

title: slug-horn
short: Properly a form of 'slogan' (a war-cry); Chatterton mistook it for a kind of horn, and Browning follows his error.
body: 'Slughorn' was an old Scots spelling of 'slogan', from Gaelic sluagh-ghairm, the battle-cry of a host. Thomas Chatterton, in his pseudo-medieval Rowley poems (Battle of Hastings), used 'slughorne' as if it were a trumpet, and the OED records this as an erroneous sense. Browning takes it over, so Roland 'blows' a horn. The word thus combines two meanings: a horn, as Roland sounds in the Chanson de Roland, and, by origin, a defiant war-cry. That is just what he utters: the poem's own title.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'slughorn, n.'
Thomas Chatterton, 'The Battle of Hastings' (Rowley poems, 1777)

anchor: Childe Roland to the Dark Tower
title: Childe Roland
short: 'Childe' was a title for a young man of noble birth not yet knighted; Roland recalls the hero of the Chanson de Roland, who blows his horn before he dies.
body: 'Childe' (as in Byron's Childe Harold) marks a candidate for knighthood. Roland is the nephew of Charlemagne in the Chanson de Roland, who at Roncesvalles refuses to blow his horn until too late, then blows it so hard that he bursts his temples. Edgar's song in Lear connects the name with the 'dark tower' of a lost ballad, which some have linked to a Scottish tale of Childe Rowland rescuing his sister from Elfland (retold by Joseph Jacobs in English Fairy Tales, 1890). Browning's ending makes the title also the poem's last words: the knight names himself in the third person, as if signing the story.

sources.cite: Shakespeare, King Lear 3.4 (Edgar as Poor Tom: 'Child Rowland to the dark tower came')
'Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came', Wikipedia (composition date, Browning's comments, critical readings)
Joseph Jacobs, English Fairy Tales (1890), 'Childe Rowland'

title: What does the ending mean?
short: Browning declined to explain it; critics read the last blast as triumph in failure, futility, damnation, or the poet's confrontation with his precursors.
body: Browning said the poem came upon him 'as a kind of dream' and refused to supply an allegory. W. L. Phelps listed three readings: success through failure, the futility of the quest, and the Tower as damnation. DeVane traced the scenery to Lairesse's Art of Painting and to Browning's reading. Harold Bloom calls the poem a 'loving critique' of Shelley and reads Roland as questing for his own failure. Others stress the courage of the gesture: 'Dauntless' he sounds the horn knowing the end. The poem breaks off before any combat, so it ends in the act of announcing, and readers must decide whether that counts as victory.
